01 / THE PEDAGOGY

A cycle for becoming
an adaptive legal writer.

Writing is recursive. Each phase makes a different kind of judgement teachable. Select a phase to explore the student's work and the bounded role of AI.

Plan · Draft · Test · Revise · Verify · Reflect. Revisit earlier choices whenever the text or the legal problem demands it.

THE ARGUMENT

Teach the decisions that make
legal writing work.

01

Genre shapes the task.

A problem answer, memorandum, submission and client letter do different work. Students need to understand how audience, purpose and authority shape each text.

02

Process can be taught.

Planning, monitoring and revising are strategies to practise explicitly. Comments on a finished product leave too much of that process invisible.

03

Judgement needs calibration.

Students must learn to explain when and why a writing choice works, diagnose a draft against criteria and carry feedback into the next task.

04

AI use needs a learning purpose.

Comparison, critique and simulated readers can expose choices for scrutiny. Fluent model output cannot stand in for a student's legal reasoning or source verification.

02 / INSIDE THE BOOK

Twelve chapters.
One connected method.

From learning to write law to designing a curriculum that transfers. Choose a part, then select a chapter.

03 / THE TEACHING, IN PRACTICE

Beyond
“use IRAC”.

Chapter 4 is the proposed sample for commissioning review. Explore how genre analysis, metacognition, feedback and bounded AI use become a teachable sequence.

AN ILLUSTRATIVE ACTIVITY PROMPT

The adversarial reader.

Adapted from the sample-chapter activity. Use with the student's own reasoning map or paragraph, public hypothetical material and an institutionally permitted tool. This page demonstrates the activity; it does not send content to an AI model.

Act as an adversarial reader of my reasoning map or paragraph.

Identify assumptions, missing counterarguments and ambiguous reasoning steps. Ask questions that help me test my own analysis.

Do not write the answer, invent facts, suggest cases or provide legal authorities. Do not treat any legal claim as verified.

I will classify your suggestions, verify the relevant propositions against primary materials and explain which suggestions I accept or reject.
04 / THE EVIDENCE

Evidence-led.
Limits included.

The proposal draws on legal-writing studies, strategy instruction, genre research and emerging AI evidence. Filter the studies and open each card for its teaching implication and limitations.

The evidence boundary. Legal-writing research is smaller and more jurisdictionally varied than the general writing literature. GenAI evidence is young. Findings below are reported in the proposal; population, study design and measured outcomes constrain their transfer to legal education. Effect sizes from different studies are not directly comparable.
05 / THE PUBLISHING OPPORTUNITY

The educator-facing
companion.

A staff text and professional resource for teaching teams, curriculum designers and legal-writing educators. Its distinctive contribution is a method for teaching students to become adaptive legal writers.

Comparison basis: publisher descriptions and publicly available contents reported in the proposal, rather than a full-text audit. Stronger claims about omissions require checking publisher copies. Existing research and writing texts already address aspects of AI.

A different primary reader.

Unit coordinators, lecturers, tutors, legal-writing teachers, clinical educators, academic developers and program leaders. Also relevant to JD and postgraduate teaching, librarians and transition-to-practice programs.

Adoption through teaching practice.

A resource for tutor induction, tutorial preparation, staff development, curriculum renewal and assessment redesign. Individual chapters can support teaching teams and selected postgraduate learning.

A durable organising principle.

Genre, self-regulation, verification and human responsibility outlast individual interfaces. The Australian centre provides a clear home-market identity, with transferability across other legal-education contexts.

06 / FROM BOOK TO CLASSROOM

A book designed
to be used.

Every chapter would combine a genre lens, a metacognitive checkpoint, work to complete before AI, a bounded activity, a verification protocol, an assessment move, a 20-minute teaching routine and common failure modes.

Proposed manuscript specifications
ManuscriptApproximately 85,000 words; around 320 pages, plus digital educator resources.
Structure12 chapters in four parts, with annotated examples, diagrams, tables and teaching routines.
DeliveryIndicatively 12 months from contract, subject to agreement on scope, co-authorship and resources.
UpdatesKeep volatile, tool-specific material online; minimise interface screenshots and model names in print.

  • 01Editable lesson plans

Proposed companion resources, rather than completed downloads. These assets could support the publisher's lecturer and teaching-team resource model.

Stable responsibilities. Changing tools.

Verify the authority.

Check cases, legislation, quotations, pinpoint references and propositions against authoritative material. Treat model output as an unverified claim.

Protect the material.

Distinguish public hypothetical content from confidential, personal, privileged or protected information before selecting an AI workflow.

Keep responsibility human-led.

Align use and disclosure with the applicable assessment and professional requirements. Students remain responsible for the reasoning and final text.
